title: Writing & Email Language
description: Formal phrases, connectors, and vocabulary for professional emails, reports, and documents.

words.definitionEn: To confirm receipt of something, or to recognise and accept that something is true.
words.exampleSentence: I am writing to acknowledge receipt of your proposal.
words.nuance: Acknowledging receipt is a professional courtesy — it tells the sender you have received their communication.
words.realLifeTask: Begin email replies with 'Thank you for your email. I acknowledge receipt of…' in formal contexts.

words.definitionEn: To communicate or express an idea, feeling, or message through writing or speech.
words.exampleSentence: I hope this letter conveys the urgency of the matter.
words.nuance: More formal than 'show' or 'tell' — preferred in professional writing.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'I hope this conveys…' to check alignment in formal emails.

words.definitionEn: Expressed clearly and briefly, without unnecessary words.
words.exampleSentence: Please keep the executive summary succinct — no more than half a page.
words.nuance: Succinctness is a valued skill in business writing — brevity respects the reader's time.
words.realLifeTask: Aim for succinct emails: state your purpose in the first sentence.

words.definitionEn: Directly relevant and applicable to the matter being discussed.
words.exampleSentence: Please include only pertinent information in the report.
words.nuance: Stronger than 'relevant' — implies something is both relevant and important.
words.realLifeTask: Filter your reports: only include pertinent data to avoid information overload.

words.definitionEn: To spread or distribute information widely to a group or audience.
words.exampleSentence: The results will be disseminated to all team leaders by Friday.
words.nuance: Formal alternative to 'share' — implies systematic, wide distribution.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'disseminate' in memos: 'Please disseminate this update to your teams.'

words.definitionEn: To gather information from various sources and organise it into a single document.
words.exampleSentence: I've compiled feedback from all departments into this report.
words.nuance: Implies organisation and synthesis — not just collecting but making sense of data.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'compiled' in report introductions: 'This document compiles findings from…'

words.definitionEn: To write a preliminary version of a document that will be reviewed and revised.
words.exampleSentence: I'll draft the proposal this afternoon and send it for your review.
words.nuance: A 'draft' signals the document is not final — always label drafts clearly.
words.realLifeTask: Label documents clearly: 'DRAFT v1 – not for distribution' to avoid confusion.

words.definitionEn: To carefully read a document to check for and correct errors in spelling, grammar, and punctuation.
words.exampleSentence: Always proofread your emails before sending them to clients.
words.nuance: Proofreading is the final quality check — done after all content revisions are complete.
words.realLifeTask: Build a habit: never send important documents without proofreading once.

words.definitionEn: To send or distribute a document, email, or notice to a group of people.
words.exampleSentence: Could you circulate the agenda before the meeting tomorrow?
words.nuance: Implies systematic distribution to a defined list — more formal than 'send around'.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'Please circulate' when distributing documents to a team or committee.

words.definitionEn: A formal phrase used to reference and confirm what was discussed in a previous conversation.
words.exampleSentence: Per our conversation yesterday, I'm attaching the revised contract.
words.nuance: Creates a paper trail — signals that the email confirms something already verbally agreed.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'as per our discussion' or 'following our call' in follow-up emails.

words.definitionEn: A formal phrase used to indicate that a document or file is attached to an email.
words.exampleSentence: Please find attached the signed agreement for your records.
words.nuance: Formal and traditional — modern alternatives include 'I've attached' or 'attached you'll find'.
words.realLifeTask: Mention the attachment by name: 'Please find attached the Q3 Report.pdf.'

words.definitionEn: From this point on; used to describe how things will be done in the future.
words.exampleSentence: Going forward, all requests should be submitted via the new portal.
words.nuance: Very common in business — marks a change in process or expectation from now on.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'going forward' to establish new procedures: 'Going forward, please copy me on all client emails.'

words.definitionEn: In accordance with; following the instructions or agreement specified.
words.exampleSentence: As per the terms of the agreement, payment is due within 30 days.
words.nuance: Formal but sometimes seen as passive-aggressive — use carefully in conflict situations.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'as per the attached document' to refer readers to specific written evidence.

words.definitionEn: Despite or in spite of a particular factor or circumstance.
words.exampleSentence: Notwithstanding the delay, the project remains on budget.
words.nuance: Highly formal — common in legal and contractual documents but rarely in everyday emails.
words.realLifeTask: Reserve 'notwithstanding' for legal, contractual, or very formal business writing.

words.definitionEn: Instead of; as a substitute or replacement for something.
words.exampleSentence: You will receive time off in lieu of overtime payment.
words.nuance: Common in HR and legal contexts — 'time off in lieu' (TOIL) is a standard HR term.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'in lieu of' in HR communications about alternative compensation.

words.definitionEn: As a result of this communication; used in formal declarations and legal documents.
words.exampleSentence: You are hereby notified of the changes to your contract.
words.nuance: Strictly formal and legal — rarely appropriate in everyday business emails.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'hereby' in formal notices, legal documents, and official declarations only.

words.definitionEn: In accordance with; following or as a result of a rule, agreement, or instruction.
words.exampleSentence: Pursuant to our earlier agreement, we are proceeding with the acquisition.
words.nuance: Legal/formal language — common in contracts and official correspondence.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'pursuant to' in legal or contractual emails to reference specific clauses.

words.definitionEn: A warning, condition, or qualification attached to a statement or agreement.
words.exampleSentence: The report is positive, but there's one important caveat — the data is six months old.
words.nuance: Adding a caveat shows intellectual honesty — you're flagging a limitation or risk.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'with one caveat' to flag important limitations in your reports or recommendations.

words.definitionEn: Standardised, often repeated language used in documents, contracts, or communications.
words.exampleSentence: The legal team added the standard boilerplate disclaimer to all outgoing contracts.
words.nuance: Can be pejorative — 'boilerplate response' implies a lazy, generic answer.
words.realLifeTask: Avoid boilerplate in client emails — personalise key sections to show genuine engagement.

words.definitionEn: A concise overview of a longer document, designed to give busy decision-makers the key information.
words.exampleSentence: The executive summary should cover the main findings in no more than two pages.
words.nuance: Written for senior audiences who may not read the full report — make it standalone and clear.
words.realLifeTask: Always include an executive summary in reports over 5 pages; write it last but place it first.

words.definitionEn: The time required to complete a task or process from start to finish.
words.exampleSentence: What's your expected turnaround time for the revised proposal?
words.nuance: Often abbreviated to TAT in internal communications — sets clear expectations.
words.realLifeTask: Always specify turnaround time in project briefs and client proposals.

words.definitionEn: To mark up or edit a document by showing proposed changes, typically in red.
words.exampleSentence: The lawyer redlined the contract and sent it back with suggested amendments.
words.nuance: Standard in legal and contract negotiations — implies detailed, tracked changes.
words.realLifeTask: Ask 'Can you redline the contract and send it back?' in legal document reviews.

words.definitionEn: The most important or fundamental point, often the final conclusion or financial result.
words.exampleSentence: The bottom line is that we need to cut costs by 15% this quarter.
words.nuance: Originally financial (net profit line), now widely used for 'the main point'. Use to cut to the chase.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'the bottom line is…' to summarise your recommendation clearly and directly.

words.definitionEn: To send a copy of an email to additional recipients, or the act of doing so.
words.exampleSentence: Please cc me on all client correspondence going forward.
words.nuance: CC (carbon copy) is visible; BCC (blind carbon copy) is not. Use BCC carefully to avoid transparency issues.
words.realLifeTask: Use cc strategically — over-cc'ing creates noise; under-cc'ing causes information gaps.

words.definitionEn: Specific tasks or next steps assigned to people, typically resulting from a meeting or discussion.
words.exampleSentence: Here's a summary of the action items from today's meeting, with owners and due dates.
words.nuance: Always include owner + deadline — 'action items' without these rarely get done.
words.realLifeTask: Send meeting summaries with a clear 'Action Items' table: item | owner | due date.

words.definitionEn: To give formal approval or authorisation to a document, plan, or expenditure.
words.exampleSentence: I need the CFO to sign off on the budget before we proceed.
words.nuance: Signals formal, official approval — without it, nothing moves forward.
words.realLifeTask: Build sign-off into your project timelines — who needs to approve and by when?

words.definitionEn: To include someone in a communication or email thread so they are kept informed.
words.exampleSentence: Could you loop in Sarah from finance? She'll need to know about this.
words.nuance: Common in email culture — ensures relevant people stay informed without separate emails.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'looping in' in email threads: 'Looping in Tom, who can advise on the legal side.'

words.definitionEn: To check on the progress of something, or to send a subsequent communication after an initial one.
words.exampleSentence: I'll follow up with the client on Monday if we haven't heard back.
words.nuance: A polite follow-up after 3-5 business days is standard and professional.
words.realLifeTask: Set a follow-up reminder for every email awaiting a response — don't let things fall through the cracks.

words.definitionEn: In South Asian business English: to reply or respond (to an email). In standard English: to return to a previous state.
words.exampleSentence: Please revert with your confirmation by Thursday. (Indian/South Asian business English)
words.nuance: Common in South Asian business contexts; in global English it usually means 'return to a previous state'.
words.realLifeTask: If writing for global audiences, use 'please respond' or 'please reply' to avoid confusion.

words.definitionEn: A formal phrase used to introduce the final point or conclusion of a letter, email, or presentation.
words.exampleSentence: In closing, I would like to thank all of you for your continued support.
words.nuance: Signals the end is near — prepares readers for the final, usually important, point.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'in closing' to signal your wrap-up in formal letters or presentations.

words.definitionEn: A formal salutation used when the specific recipient is unknown.
words.exampleSentence: To Whom It May Concern: I am writing to enquire about your services.
words.nuance: Old-fashioned but still used for formal letters to unknown recipients. 'Dear Hiring Manager' is now preferred for job applications.
words.realLifeTask: Avoid 'To Whom It May Concern' when you can find the specific person's name — personalise when possible.

words.definitionEn: Conditional on; dependent on a particular thing happening or being true.
words.exampleSentence: The offer is subject to board approval and satisfactory due diligence.
words.nuance: Critical in contracts and proposals — 'subject to' signals a condition that must be met.
words.realLifeTask: Always specify what a commitment is 'subject to' so there are no surprises later.

words.definitionEn: Awaiting completion, decision, or approval; not yet resolved.
words.exampleSentence: The contract is still pending legal review.
words.nuance: Useful in status updates — 'pending' signals something is in progress but not done.
words.realLifeTask: Use a 'PENDING' label in project trackers to flag items awaiting action.

words.definitionEn: Not yet completed, paid, or resolved — still to be dealt with.
words.exampleSentence: There are three outstanding invoices from Q2 that need to be settled.
words.nuance: Financial context: unpaid. General: incomplete. Also means 'excellent' — context matters!
words.realLifeTask: Send 'outstanding invoice' reminders clearly and professionally to maintain cash flow.

words.definitionEn: To add something to the end of a document or piece of writing.
words.exampleSentence: I have appended the full data set at the end of this report.
words.nuance: More formal than 'add' — used for attachments, footnotes, or annexures.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'appended' when referring to supplementary data: 'see the appended table for full figures'.

words.definitionEn: To explain something in more detail, adding clarity or further information in writing.
words.exampleSentence: The report will elaborate on the risks identified during phase one.
words.nuance: Used in writing to signal that more detail follows — sets reader expectations.
words.realLifeTask: Write 'Section 3 elaborates on these findings' to guide readers through your document.

words.definitionEn: Following or consistent with rules, requirements, or instructions.
words.exampleSentence: In accordance with company policy, all expenses must be submitted within 30 days.
words.nuance: Standard in policy, legal, and regulatory communications — signals compliance.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'in accordance with' when citing policy or regulation to add formal authority.

words.definitionEn: A polite way to ask someone to do something as soon as they are able to.
words.exampleSentence: Please respond at your earliest convenience so we can proceed.
words.nuance: Polite but sometimes vague — if urgency is real, add a specific deadline instead.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'at your earliest convenience' for non-urgent but important requests — add a date if it's time-sensitive.

words.term: I trust this finds you well
words.definitionEn: A formal email opener expressing hope that the recipient is doing well.
words.exampleSentence: I trust this email finds you well. I am writing to follow up on our last conversation.
synonyms: I hope this email finds you well
words.nuance: Traditional and formal — considered warm by some, formulaic by others. Know your audience.
words.realLifeTask: Use formal email openers in initial contact with senior or external stakeholders.

words.definitionEn: A polite adverb used in formal requests, meaning 'please' or 'in a courteous manner'.
words.exampleSentence: Kindly note that the office will be closed on Monday.
words.nuance: Common in South Asian and African business English; in British English, 'please' is more natural.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'please' in most formal emails — save 'kindly' for very formal notices or international contexts.

words.definitionEn: Indicating that the information or document provided is for the recipient to use or keep.
words.exampleSentence: I've attached the original agreement for your reference.
words.nuance: Standard email phrase — implies the attachment is informational, not requiring action.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'for your reference' when attaching documents that provide background, not requiring action.
